title: Deadly Design: How a one-ton pylon fell-what the city knew all along - NewsBreak
text: ST. LOUIS – It was a tragedy that could have been prevented. Jan Torissi-Mokwa died in 2018—simply driving home on Forest Park Parkway. A one-ton pylon came crashing down on her after having been hit by a driver above on the Lindell/Union bridge. After it happened, FOX 2 brought investigative reports, revealing previous crashes that sent rock tumbling below. FOX 2 continued digging, with a 2019 report on how city leaders feared disaster before the fatal crash—including an email warning from a street commissioner pleading, “please make it safe.” Thanks for signing up! Watch for us in your inbox. Subscribe Now “They had the answer,” trial attorney Neil Bruntrager said. Bruntrager and his co-counsel Amy Boltzman spent $51,000 and seven years getting answers that led to Monday’s half-a-million-dollar settlement. “…What they knew, when they knew it and what they could have done to remedy the situation,” Bruntrager said. They found four similar incidents occurred in just the 12 months prior to Mokwa’s. “The bureaucracy is what surprised me the most because they knew from the time it was built in 1910 it was an ornamental handrail,” Bruntrager said. This model was not much different from a flimsy version that Bruntrager created and demonstrated. Original construction plans, obtained by FOX 2 back in 2019, revealed the one-ton pylons were never anchored to the bridge and that it was intended to be a roundabout, with a garden in the center. When driver Damaya Love hit the bridge wall traveling an estimated 14-28 mph, Bruntrager said the result was what city leaders had been concerned about for years. “Their argument was it’s too expensive to do it,” Bruntrager said. Too expensive to put up jersey barriers that are in place today “that cost them nothing,” according to Bruntrager. It may not look like much to the public. Bruntrager’s research found “they’re crashworthy—up to a ¾ ton truck going 45 mph—that has, since that day, prevented any further incidents.” The city of St. Louis declined to talk on camera with FOX 2 but did say more changes are coming. The bridge is currently in a design phase for a major makeover, with construction set to begin next year. For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to FOX 2.
